title: 1 Samuel 22:20–23
context: One priest escapes: Abiathar, son of Ahimelech, flees to David and tells him what Saul has done. David admits that he knew Doeg would report him and takes responsibility for the deaths. He promises Abiathar protection, and from this point the priest with the ephod travels with David.

verses.text: One of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David.
verses.arminianNotes: Abiathar alone escapes and flees to David. Arminian readers see God preserving a remnant even in disaster, and note Abiathar's choice to cast his lot with the fugitive David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Abiathar later brings the ephod to David (23:6). The priestly line God preserves now joins the true king, so God's means of guidance passes from Saul's court to David.

verses.text: Abiathar told David that Saul had slain the LORD’s priests.
verses.arminianNotes: Abiathar tells David that Saul has killed the LORD's priests. Arminian readers note the grief and weight of this news, which confronts David with the consequences of choices made at Nob.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the news shows how completely Saul has broken with God. A king who murders God's priests has rejected the very worship he was meant to protect.

verses.text: David said to Abiathar, “I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I am responsible for the death of all the persons of your father’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: "I am responsible for the death of all the persons of your father's house." Arminian readers see genuine repentance: David owns the consequences of his deception rather than blaming Saul or Doeg alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see honest confession. Saul and Doeg bear the guilt of murder, yet David acknowledges his share. Both traditions see in this a model of taking responsibility before God.

verses.text: Stay with me. Don’t be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. You will be safe with me.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Stay with me," David says, and "You will be safe with me." Arminian readers see David offering protection and fellowship, a leader who shares danger with those who suffer alongside him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David's promise rests on his confidence in God's purpose for him. Many see a faint foreshadowing of the greater Son of David who shelters those who come to him, though the text does not draw that link.
